text:
SIX ALLIGATORS



The earliest piece of writing that I can find in my Google Drive is when I was twelve. At the risk of coming off like a recipe blog with useless preamble, I want to note that it’s a little gratifying to see that ten years later, my writing quality has improved a bit.





Generally speaking, it’s become little less dramatic, and I’m also better now at deciding on names as opposed to using PERSON1 placeholders. My spelling blindspots continue to surprise me though, and I can’t say if my writing now has improved more as a result of what I read, as opposed to practicing the craft. Sometimes I write and write and write, and rereading such pieces makes me understand why some people believe that God is speaking through them. Brigham Young and I, two peas (prophets?) in a pod. Not that I’ve written anything especially profound or surprising in any one piece, but there is something sneakily transient about things I’ve written.
However in-control I am of my writing or not, it has always been a place of expression for me, and after taking one of my last general education classes in university on writing, I was moved by good teaching (thank you Nico!), good reading, and great conversation with my classmates to dig a little deeper into it, and to also perhaps share with those around me. May something within my ramblings bring you some sort of deeper thought, or at the very least, a chuckle.
- katinka

title: zine 5
text:
April 30, 2026. 9:34AM.
Feeling like a serif font today. Also feeling the fucked up Google Docs margins today, although that bit wasn’t by design. Feeling like a paragraph format too! No artsy line breaks today. ALSO feeling caffeinated—I got a latte at the coffee shop, and since my desire to flex my Chinese was larger than my desire for a flat white, the extra liquid is sloshing around in my empty gut like a laxative promise. (Superb coffee by the way, beans are roasted and ground on site and they have floppy sacks of coffee beans as decor on the side to emphasize this). This place is sitting at the bottom of a hostel, and because of this fact, I get to people-watch all the white people speak Chinese, perhaps as good as me! No way to tell through the short interaction of a coffee order, but I like to imagine.
Can you tell I’m caffeinated with that paragraph? I suspect that if I don’t write and post this all in one go, this zine will perish within the depths of draft untitled documents. I’m also in the midst, as per usual, of avoiding additional responsibilities in favor of what I like to think of as Creative Expression And The Recording of Life Lived.



Fig. 1. Current POV.


Perhaps the cappuccino is a good way to stress test my lactose intolerance. Risky business while travelling to be honest but given the accessibility of public bathrooms in Taiwan, perhaps not so bad after all. Anyhow: on the to-do list (which really manifests as a to-avoid list) is answering two emails, the first which was sent to me two days ago and the second which was sent to me two weeks ago, a job application, a survey to fill out, a school bill to pay, and another email (whoops) that I forgot to account for earlier in this sentence, sent to me sometime last night. The post-grad feeling is that of the constant loose ends. But tying loose ends that I to be fair am the origin of, so I’m not complaining.
A couple just came up to the counter. By the shape of their noses, I think they’re siblings, but they’re also about 70 years old so I wonder who is travelling with their siblings at that age? Hopefully me! I’ve also heard the theory that couples grow to look like each other with age. But bone structure seems like a bit of a stretch. Perhaps they got matching rhinoplasties.
Enough speculation though…this open Google Doc has the aura of work at this coffee shop, but time to actually get back to work. I hope I come across a cat today.

title: ZINE 2
text:
Saturday 11:57pm
Here’s to a zine, zine 2, zine 2.0, the second of the lot
(The 2 suggesting some sort of progression, but really the best zines I argue are a digression, so the linear relationship of numbers fail to encapsulate the spiraling and meandering
A lack of relation between these, let’s be honest, even with the author)

Here’s to looking at things,
Twice!
Like this artichoke here
Escaped my judgement unscathed the first time
But a second look has me thinking a little too much about vaginally reminiscent objects
Second look, second thought—

Hm.
Second thoughts are never as punchy as first thoughts
Nor as rational as the third
But they are arguably the most interesting of the lot
And belong best on a napkin or in the notes app,
To be mulled on by third thoughts,
Masticated by fourths,
And unfortunately ruined by fifths, so really they should be kept under wraps and not considered too strongly

Saturday 1:04am
Sometimes when I look at small kids, I get the feeling that they are the only thing Inherently good and true left in this world
Everyone else around is old
Jaded
Their diverging fig’s tree of a path, easily judged
What they chose to do, what they have not

title: On Casual Intimacy
text:
On My Oral Hygienist
A 9am appointment I am never mentally ready for
After 11am starts to my day in school, a 9am really feels like a 7am
Too early to muster up the energy to small talk, too late to have an excuse to sit in the dentists chair
Face slack, eyes glazed
(and too old to boot)
Staring ideally at the fish painted on the ceiling
But really, what I want to do is stare into the eyes of my hygienist.
Okay, not like that!
She (Joanne?) always has mascara on, which I just want to peruse the application of
Without the forced intimacy of prolonged eye contact
Or giving myself the reputation of Patrick Bateman serial killer energy
She has gray eyes too
Or maybe blue
See, I would know for sure if more solid eye contact was made! But it is not to be.


INTERMISSION
On Emails
Answering emails was a scary, procrastinating task
To unpack, it probably relates to taking responsibility, accountability, or irrevocability
But:
At some undetermined point in time,
I suddenly became The Emailer, not the Emailee
Being the replier has become a thing of the past
A sheep morphed into a wolf, puzzled by this transformation
(the Öh My God Why Must I Answer This Email feeling has become replaced by a new sinking-stomach sensation, called Oh My God Why Isn’t There An Unsend Email Option)
Anyhow
I think I lose a little bit of humanity every time I google
“Template for follow-up emails”
The very best corporate secretary in me comes out, an alternate timeline of being an overworked assistant working at the front desk
(of the Runway Magazine?)
Working (for….Miranda Priestly?) Ideally, the best dressed in the office
Living out a 2006 comedy-drama dream


12.18.2023
One of my favorite markers of casual intimacy is telling friends I made some food today with something that they’re allergic to. (e.g., almonds biscotti to the poor oafs allergic to nuts.) I think it’s neat to remind them that (a) I know what kills you (b) and I opted not act on it, at least today

title: After School
text:
cooking all day, small hands red and
fingers curled, fermenting
in porcelain bowls and black vinegar tang
uncountable spoons in jars with red lids

cracked brown eggshells
oh / oh
i do not know
the steps to
this unwritten recipe
why would i
i’ve never had to make it / alone
the sweetness
lingers /
i become a child / once more
soup ladled out with heart
“come eat—


swollen tension ballooning
feelings all day
sourness unmellowed by time
histories written in sticky residues

i come home and the air whispers
oh.
[ ]
this dance again
of rupture to come
so familiar / my tongue knows this taste
with my thoughts
of bitter thoughts
linger
once more / déjà vu
o these labors of love
it’ll grow cold”

title: Searching for Truth
text:
Equidistant := people waiting for the 1 on Strathmore
The only truth I feel sure of these days is that nothing is universally true anymore, for two reasons: (1) The joy of critical thinking1 also means that with a few layers of questioning, I can conjure some edge case that makes a generalization grossly untrue for someone somewhere, and (2) In fact, we live in such a globalized world that our spheres of understanding, once small and local, have grown to encompass all the knowledge that can be shared on the internet. We could have, as peasants-serfs on a wheat farm, made some pretty generalizing statements in good faith about our limited lives. Now though? Good luck doing that without getting cancelled.
Yet the human tendency to pick up on patterns is unavoidable. In each new environment, we find that there’s a set of rules for survival: the assumptions of what is valued, the requirements to gain within the system, and unspoken social norms. Frustratingly though, each new environment that you enter has new rules, and goddamn if they aren’t complicated and moreover different from the last set.
Garden of Eden
The earliest I can really recall this was in my middle school experience, likely because this is when our brains really start developing nuanced awareness of social dynamics. Here, I had emerged from elementary school scampering to find my footing in new classes, new teachers, and friends scattered to the four winds. I was also granted the luxurious autonomy in owning my very first piece of space, otherwise known as the combination locker—in this locker I stored my first piece of property that my mom didn’t know about. Namely, a tin of Altoids that my friend procured for me, paid for through our joint venture of selling paper ninja stars to affluent boys who bought them, a quarter a piece.
The rules? Do your homework, and you’ll do well in class. Put yourself out there to find new friends, because your old ones are doing the same. Realize that people want things sometimes (paper ninja stars), and you can gain by providing those needs. By the end of middle school, I found myself with favorite teachers and subjects, enjoying the rewards from engaging in capitalistic exchange of value, and in a group of friends with whom I obnoxiously sang musicals through the halls.
The Rude Awakening
High school was when this friend group which I so loved started fracturing. A drawn-out heartbreak: high school merged two nearby middle schools together, and upon the introduction of outside influences, I learned what it means to grow apart from friends, the nasty feelings of friend-friend tensions, and what it feels like to be left out. I started witnessing the start of social stratification between students in Advanced Placement classes and those not, one that became more and more pronounced through my years of high school. And I learned a hell of a lot about European history—Degas’s dancers and the 1848 revolutions in Africa stay somehow rent-free in my head even today.
The rules for survival had changed. Put yourself out there to find new friends, because your old ones are doing the same, because possibly they don’t like you anymore (for reasons that you might not be able to understand), or because they met someone they just like more. Your academic effort is now relative rather than absolute; you must compete to not get left behind. College applications spelled out to me in no uncertain terms that spots in university were highly limited, and highly coveted by my immediate peers. Whatever rules of middle school I thought were true, add a qualifier on them, stick some edge cases on them, double the complexity. On top of parsing through these new rules—puberty to boot.
The Salad Bar at Olive Garden
College? That’s where I watched the subjectivity of reality start to emerge when comparing my life to, say, my dorm neighbor. We might live entirely different lives, from the clubs we opted-in to join, to the amount of classes we decided to go to or not, to the dietary decisions we had the liberties to make. Carrots and sticks though: no longer did I need to ask to go to the bathroom, but with that same freedom came the responsibility of realizing Actions Have Consequences. Not like this rule didn’t exist in middle or high school, but college, with its hellish freedom and sky’s-the-limit options, warranted the all-caps emphasis.
Also entirely totaled now was the general effort-to-achievement relationship, once so reliable in my K12 years. I watched people nail their job interviews and secure their return offers, with their efforts bearing a frustratingly loose (sometimes even inverse) relationship with GPA and studying time. New sheriff in town: if you want to find success, know what you want, know which of your current efforts are relevant to getting what you want, and know what is irrelevant and should be ignored.2
What now? And now, post-college, I’m in a new workplace, trying to figure it out, again. The mapping of how much pay to expect based on tangible skills or intelligence or impact eludes any sort of cartography, at least in my immediate workplace. And the rules to happiness too, have a karmic non-linearity that I’ve yet to explicate—those who got what they wanted in college don’t necessarily seem the most content for instance, nor any of those who have hit classic young-adult milestones of partners or moving out.
Whoever you are, reading this piece, your middle school, high school, and college experiences more likely than not followed entirely different rules for survival than the ones I had. Cultural background, personal values, economic circumstances, there is such a kaleidoscope of factors that change how we make sense of the world. It’s a wonder that we’re able to relate to each other and coexist as humans with all these differences in experiences!
But that is what makes socializing so fun: seeing the human in each other through comparing each of paths. So even if there is no universal truth, I’d like to highlight the art of being curious, and making those generalizations anyway. I’m saying this as someone who has found much joy in creating metaphors and similes, comparing situations between people and coming together to find some sort of common truth.3 These generalizations help situate myself within the world, and also construct my own understanding of the world. Sometimes they’re not true, but sometimes they are useful for my immediate environment, such as the Garden of Eden, the Rude Awakening, the Salad Bar. These pet understandings make sense to me within the context of this piece of writing, and perhaps not much further than that, but they are still helpful in providing structure and understanding.
Beyond our personal generalizations, it’s through talking with others about our experiences in life that we may touch on this wonderful feeling of constructing a common understanding of the world. Consider the concept of collective memory, which Wikipedia defines as a shared set of memories, knowledge, and information crucial to a social group’s identity. Collective understanding takes this collective memory one step further, and extrapolates them into frameworks that make sense of the world and how it works. That’s the joy of the post-event debrief, or a moral debate on a hypothetical. Some of my most wonderful friendships have been formed out of this catharsis of discovery, curiosity, and disagreement, trying to pin down the rules of the world and failing, but enjoying the process anyways. So gossip away, question away, share experiences and always, stay curious about not just the world, but the people that are experiencing this world with you, together.

title: The Uses of Grief in Climate Change Rhetoric
text:
LA fires, from out my friend’s dorm window


Something that reliably grinds my gears: bestowed faith upon our generation that we will solve The Climate Change Issue. It comes usually in the form of well meaning older adults seeing some motivated kids doing something—anything, really—that is vaguely environmental. Extra points if you are young. Extra extra points if you involve other people! Extra extra extra points if you do something that an adult was supposed to do!
“Oh my, you are so smart and talented and I have so much faith in you to solve climate change! It’s the biggest problem of your generation!”
Biggest. Problem. Of my generation.
(Dear reader: I hope you can tell that this is a touchy subject.)
I have nothing against the people who espouse these sentiments, but the rollercoaster of grief that I’ve gone through from being born into a world I’ve been told is going to go up in flames within my lifetime, to be so trivially absolved to be a problem of my generation– it does piss me off just a bit.
Let’s Marty McFly this back to, say 2016. Flashback to me, sitting in 6th grade science class, learning about climate change. Glaciers, emaciated polar bears, the little greenhouse gas-earth diagram with the reflecting sun rays if you know what I’m referring to: “Congrats, this nice world you grew up in isn’t going to exist in fifty years!”
But no shock there. When you’re young, you swallow things whole as they come. As such, I wasn’t even allowed the liberty of shock when learning about climate change. Climate change was taught as a fact of life. Unit 6: Photosynthesis, followed by Unit 7: Existential Threat to the Future. (Side note/silver lining: climate change education may be a little different now.
We know more about the problem and know a little more about what to do to fix it, or at least a roadmap of goals we must hit, so hopefully education isn’t so doom-and-gloom anymore and is hopefully a little more trauma-informed. But this is dependent on where you grew up and the education system there. I digress.)
But onto the next stage: anger. Luckily, given the ubiquitous nature of carbon dioxide emissions, there is no shortage of people to blame: “Look at Big Oil! They knew in the 1950s, why didn’t they do anything! Look at policy makers, they aren’t lifting a finger! Look at the lousy, unscientific Republicans! Look at the fear-mongering Democrats!”
Yet how can you really blame one person? Each person only does the best that they can do. It’s really the overlapping systems of values and economic growth that have caused us to get where we are today…But at what point does a group of people become a system? Where does the line of responsibility get drawn? Anger either becomes diffuse, withering into gray apathy, or it becomes accusatory and fingerpointing toward pieces of the puzzle that don’t really compromise the whole. This is one that took me a long time to learn, often with a lot of internalized resentment toward various bad actors that really just were acting as expected within the constraints of our society.
Ok, what’s next? Bargaining: “Here’s the deal: climate change is very much a huge problem, primarily caused by global warming. It comes from everybody’s carbon footprint! So, if you reduce your own carbon footprint, you’ll be doing your part to save the planet!”
A real hole was popped in this bubble when I learned that fossil fuel companies were the ones who popularized this “carbon footprint” concept, potentially to shift blame from organizations to individuals. As I learned more about the problem and different frameworks of blame, the reality of bargaining shifted frequently: from hoping that everyone would change their behavior, to hoping that the five biggest polluting companies would be shut down, to hoping that law makers would be the ones to save us. I mean, there are so many people who could take action.
Despair strikes when I think about all the loss that is happening, that is going to happen. How do you live in a town thinking it’s going to be underwater in a few years? How do you build a house thinking it’ll just burn down? Planning for the future becomes difficult, if not pointless.
But consider finally, acceptance: “Look at this problem of your generation–you all are going to do so well in solving it!” When it’s put like that, it sure feels like a problem of my own generation! When responsibility is placed on my shoulders like that, a moment of panic and rejection ensues. A part of me also feels a sense of injustice: if I was never allowed the luxury of faith in my forebearers to provide a stable world to live in, why should I entertain the faith that my generation will right these wrongs?
You can probably spy a common thread throughout this entire process: given massive, entropic problems pervasive across space and time, the accompanying emotions are hard to process and difficult to logic out. As such, touching on climate change can often be like opening a Pandora’s box, a Thanksgiving table off-limits topic. It’s made thinking about this problem really difficult to process. Do I care about climate change? Yes, technically. But not in the same way I care about the well being of my family, or the way I care about feminist representation. There’s too many emotions to consider. So sometimes it’s easier just to put it all away.
And while you might criticize me for this perhaps avoidant mentality, what I’d really like to ask for is some optimism. Some allies who acknowledge we’re all in this dumpster fire together. No pity party, no gold stars for effort please, just a little “Let’s get to work.” Maybe that way we can move beyond the grief of mourning the future that has been lost, and start thinking about building a future.
Cheap, abundant energy from towering offshore wind turbines. Non-monoculture (multicultural?) farming. State firefighters working with indigenous tribes on wildfire management. Space elevators, geo-engineered carbon removal, lab-grown salmon, ranked-choice voting! Maybe all of this isn’t realistic, and maybe not all of it floats your boat, but let’s start dreaming and building–together.

The thing that gets me about a zine is its nonvisuality

So sharing a zine means unzipping my brain and sharing my haphazard collection of thoughts

To be known is worse than being naked.
The body is a product of the mind.
Does anyone ever read a zine and be like “brother euhhh?”

title: zine 4
text:
Wednesday, April 16. 1:36pm.
I forgot about these, until i remember them, and then I always have a brief digression about zines:
Because here’s the thing: they walk the line between being a journal entry and being public knowledge, a weird limbo to be in
How filtered do I go? How raw do I get??
A moot point however, in the grand scheme of things.

Anywho lately i’ve been thinking that job hunting is a misleading term.
It’s more along the line of beggarship methinks.
Hunting implies a sort of power,
a concept which rejections and ghostings smash with impunity.

Other thoughts as of ten minutes ago: it’s funny how white collar jobs like data analysis and sales are treated as better than plumbing. But they’re their (sorry) own form of slavery. How is being confined to one place, day in and day out, any better than being able to move around and use your hands?

I generally dislike framing capitalist workings as some evil conspiracy to enslave, weaken, coerce the masses. Not to say that isn’t the reality. But who’s to say that conspiracies are always centralized efforts though? This concept of sitting at a desk is better— maybe it is necessary to logically justify sitting on the internet, scrolling all day, slowly decomposing our brains. (All the same, I’m guilty of this. A modern vice.)

But I suppose I do see the merits of, say, data analysis, where you can abstract what you are working on. Like math: it may just be scribbles on paper, but it means something, at least to the mathematician. But the plumber too sees the workings of the pipes like their own language—I sure as hell can’t understand it!

We all speak microcosms of languages in fact, depending on where we live and the communities we occupy and the morals we hold. I speak Upper Class Western Values, how about you? I talk about investing (a privilege), I talk about carrying out my dreams (an American), I talk about the onion I ate for lunch (a bad decision). We make friends based on who we communicate with. Building our bubbles. But who can blame wanting to be heard?
